title: Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Latin Quarter Distribution has acquired world sales rights to José Dell’Acqua’s Uruguayan crime thriller “Maltrato Animal” (“Animal Budget”). 

	The
body:
Latin Quarter Distribution has acquired world sales rights to José Dell’Acqua’s Uruguayan crime thriller “Maltrato Animal” (“Animal Budget”). 

	The deal was closed after a screening of “Maltrato Animal” at Locarno’s First Look, a pix-in-post competition focused on rough-cut screenings of emerging and established talent from a territory around the world, this year Uruguay.  

	Presented in Locarno by the Agencia del Cine y el Audiovisual del Uruguay (ACAU), which is still building Uruguay’s film-TV ecosysytem, the film, currently in the editing stage, is set against the backdrop of Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis and explores a generation shaped by that pivotal moment in the country’s history. 
	

	Bankrupted by the financial crisis, a Montevideo veterinarian is pushed to desperate straits and doesn’t have enough money to eat. In order to survive, he enters a clandestine network of illegal breeding operations and pharmaceutical peddling. In this downward spiral, an unexpected encounter potentially opens a new chapter in his life.


	Produced by Dell’Acqua and German Ormaechea, the film was shot over a four-year period — one week each year — with the support of numerous Uruguayan technicians and rental companies. The project brought together many first-time department heads, including cinematographer Germán Couto and costume designer Victoria Zavaleta, as well as an entirely Uruguayan cast, according to Dell’Aqua. Developed over eight years, the film blends fiction and reality to portray a deeply personal and collective memory. 

	“‘Maltrato Animal’ was born from the need to revisit the generation that grew up during Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis,” Dell’Acqua said. “Over eight years, I wrote, directed, and produced the film, seeking to blur the boundaries between fiction and reality. It is also a celebration of the talent of a new generation of Uruguayan filmmakers, many of whom took on leading creative roles in their first feature film.” 
	

	“After such a long and personal journey with ‘Maltrato Animal,’ I’m very happy to begin this next stage with Latin Quarter Distribution,” Dell’Aqua told Variety. “Their bold approach and distinctive curation feel deeply aligned with the spirit of the film. I believe they understand the kind of cinema we are trying to make and, most importantly, have the commitment and passion to bring it to audiences beyond Uruguay.” 

	Juan G. Castro, founder and managing director of Latin Quarter Distribution, added:  “We’re excited to add ‘Maltrato Animal’ to the Latin Quarter slate. We’re always searching for new gems and distinctive voices in Latin American arthouse cinema, and José Dell’Acqua’s first feature immediately stood out to us. Discovering the film through ACAU’s presentation of Uruguayan cinema at Locarno makes this acquisition particularly meaningful, and we’re proud to support a film that showcases the talent and originality emerging from Uruguay today.” 

	Post-production on “Maltrato Animal” is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

schema.headline: Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’
description: In the Argentine Pampas, cousins Guillermina and Belinda cannot wait to grow up. When they are not swimming in the river and dancing through the lon
body:
In the Argentine Pampas, cousins Guillermina and Belinda cannot wait to grow up. When they are not swimming in the river and dancing through the long, breezy afternoons, they re-enact funeral ceremonies and feign surgery on dead animals. This quotidian desire to accelerate the inevitable passing of time animates photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti’s debut feature, “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer.”  

	Presented in world premiere in Filmmakers of the Present at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival, the film was produced by distinguished director-producer Julia Solomonoff (“Nobody’s Watching”), with financing from Mubi and Impact Partners. 
	

	Sanguinetti’s gaze follows Guille and Belinda while they grow up, fall in love, raise children and slowly drift toward separate lives over two and a half decades. The seemingly home-footage structure forms a familiar and intimate setting, in which the grainy footage narrates the life passing between the moments Sanguinetti captured as part of her extensive, decades-long photography of close cousins Guille and Belinda. 


	“We’re just like extended family now,” says the director about her relationship with the duo, spanning over 25 years. “It was really organic. I did not want to make a project about two women growing up. I just knew them and wanted to be with them.” 

	Static framing and pixelated vignettes of tranquil farmland in Sanguinetti’s work trace back to formal similarities to “Dry Leaf,” directed by Alexandre Koberidze, another Locarno title, screened in 2025. The Argentinian prairie is adorned with imaginary houses, castles and theatres as the young girls construct spontaneous, invisible cities, stories and games in which Koberidze’s likewise unseen characters could live. Lively farm animals populate the backgrounds against which Guille and Belinda confidently perform their silly and earnest singing and dancing.
	

	Although the result bears some resemblance, the two directors employ the graininess for different aesthetic reasons. In Sanguinetti’s practice, the video camera appeared as a natural prop that watched and filmed Belinda and Guille’s performances while the director captured with her photographic camera “what happens slowly in the moment.” Comparing photography to video, she says about her relationship with the first, “I’m always more in control and looking for something. With video, I could let life flow in front of me and then later think about what to retrieve or not.”

	These snapshots of life, then overlooked as common moments, might be actually foundational to one’s trajectory, as “we don’t realize that we’re defining ourselves in that moment. You can only see that when you’re at a certain distance, when you’re knowing and loving them, but you’re not being their mother.” This in turn enabled Sanguinetti to observe “patterns in the girls’ lives — what kept repeating or changing, what things they had escaped from, and what they achieved through sheer will.”

	Sanguinetti’s tender film detours through the motions of time and eventually brings fleshiness to her presence. “In the beginning, I didn’t want to be a part of it. I thought my voice would ruin it. As the time went by, I realized that I was there and I just had to accept it.”

	If women constitute the film’s heart, animals form its pulse. Neither pets nor crude products of an economy, Sanguinetti deftly places cattle, dogs and cats alongside people and land. Essential to the farmland Pampas, the girls’ grandmother repeatedly confesses to the director about the joy of taking care of chickens and their innate beauty or the bovines’ way of behaving as a tightly knit community. 

	This sentiment is personal for Sanguinetti: “I’ve always considered animals equal to humans,” adding on their importance to the rural ecosystem: “I always felt that the animals in that space were ignored. But these people are here because of the animals in that area, because there is no agriculture.”

schema.headline: Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’

title: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Filmotor has picked up world sales rights for “Letters From the Silenced Country” by Belarusian writer-director Andrei Kutsila, which has its world
body:
Filmotor has picked up world sales rights for “Letters From the Silenced Country” by Belarusian writer-director Andrei Kutsila, which has its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival.

	The partly animated documentary, screening in the Venice Open – Out of Competition section, is a portrait of contemporary Belarus told through stories of individuals who have endured imprisonment, repression and exile – voices silenced by an autocratic regime.
	

	Following Belarus’ peaceful protests in 2020, the regime’s violent crackdown left many dead, injured, imprisoned or forced into exile. The war in Ukraine triggered anti-war resistance and even harsher repression, making public dissent nearly impossible. Against this backdrop, letters became one of the few remaining connections between political prisoners and the outside world.


	The film “transforms private stories into a cinematic space of dignity, intimacy and reflection, revealing the human cost of resistance and exploring themes of sacrifice, solidarity, and survival in a country where dissenting voices have been silenced,” according to a statement.

	Here’s the synopsis: When the streets are quiet and people are afraid to even discuss politics in Belarus, letters can give us an insight into the feelings of pain, despair, love and hope.

	Each story reveals a different facet of repression. A father lives in hiding, evading surveillance to avoid arrest and separation from his daughter. A former criminal investigator breaks with the system, flees Belarus, and, in exile in Poland, faces repeated interrogations and an increasing sense of isolation and powerlessness. Kasia, a young student imprisoned for her participation in protests, turns to drawing as a means of survival – preserving her identity and expressing what cannot be spoken openly. Fifty-year-old Vitold’s story unfolds through photographs sent by a friend from home: carefully chosen fragments of a life beyond prison walls that offer moments of freedom while revealing both what is visible and what remains hidden.
	

	Kutsila is a Belarusian documentary filmmaker based in Poland. His documentaries have been screened and awarded at major international festivals, including IDFA, DOK Leipzig, Hot Docs and the Krakow Film Festival.

	His documentary “Summa” (2018) won the IDFA Award for Best Mid-Length Documentary, followed by the Silver Hobby-Horse for Best Documentary in the National Competition at the Krakow Film Festival in 2019. “When Flowers Are Not Silent” (2021) received the Best Feature Documentary Award at the Warsaw Film Festival.

	Forced to leave Belarus after the 2020 protests, Kutsila settled in Poland, where he continued his artistic development through an internship at the Łódź Film School. Over the past five years, his work has focused primarily on documenting the experiences of Belarusians living under repression and in exile.

	Michaela Čajková, founder and sales and festivals executive at Filmotor, said, “Using an innovative blend of animation, archive and personal correspondence, Kutsila crafts an essential, unforgettable portrait of human dignity against autocratic repression.”

	Producer Mirosław Dembiński, president at DocEdu Foundation, said, “Twenty years ago, I directed the film ‘Lesson of Belarusian,’ which chronicled the repression of the Lukashenko regime: street brutality by the police, mass arrests and long sentences. Since then, it’s been the same: the same batons, the same prisons, the same Lukashenko. Since 2020, it’s been even worse, because the scale of repression has become more widespread. Andrei Kutsila took on the challenge of making a documentary about political prisoners in Belarus. It’s also an artistic challenge: how to make a film about someone who can’t be filmed. I think he’s found a way.”

	“Letters From the Silenced Country” is produced by DocEdu Foundation in Poland in co-production with Moonmakers in Lithuania, and Inselfilm Produktion in Germany. It was supported by the Polish Film Institute, the Lithuanian Film Center and Connected Foundation, and was co-produced by TVP, EC1 – Lodz City of Culture and ZDF, in collaboration with ARTE and Deutsche Welle.

	The project participated in the following development programs: Young Europe, B2B, Ex Oriente, East Doc, Doc Leipzig Co-Pro Market, Movies That Metter, MDAG Industry and Watch Docs.

title: ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama
description: “I would never fall in love if I was in a good relationship.” So says one participant in the women’s church group where Copenhagen-based wife and mo
body:
“I would never fall in love if I was in a good relationship.” So says one participant in the women’s church group where Copenhagen-based wife and mother Kate (Kathrine Thorborg Johansen) confesses that she’s been having a three-year affair with another man, and doesn’t much regret it. It’s a line that sounds like sturdy, suitably Christian advice, but is it true? Kate’s husband Orla (Simon Sears) is attentive, attractive and empathetic; so is Andreas (Anders Danielsen Lie), the smart, offbeat archaeologist she’s smitten with at first sight. Alternately droll and emotionally acute, Maria Bäck’s “Brave New Love” never presents this romantic triangle as a problem with one solution; it’s considerably less judgmental than the church ladies as it gives its protagonist space to figure out if she really loves two people at once, or just loves nobody — herself included — quite enough.
	

	Premiering in the main competition at Locarno, this is an emotionally intelligent, gently wry character drama of a distinctly Scandi stripe, occupying a comparable arthouse lane to Dag Johan Haugerud’s Oslo Trilogy and recent works by Joachim Trier, albeit with a distinctly feminine point of view behind the camera. It’s not just Danielsen Lie’s reliably interesting presence that brings to mind “The Worst Person in the World” at points, as Bäck’s script (on which Trier collaborator Eskil Vogt was a consultant) ponders similar feelings of middle-class millennial female unrest in a character who simply opted for marriage and family earlier in life. Relatable and discussable, Bäck’s second narrative feature likely reps an easier sell to international distributors than her first, the darkly heightened psychodrama “Psychosis in Stockholm.”
	

	It’s on a camping trip with her family that Kate first locks eyes with Andreas — they’re both stark naked, having just swum in the same forest lake, but that’s rendered almost incidental by the telling intensity of their shared gaze. When he walks off, Kate scribbles down her number and leaves it under his towel. But then “Brave New Love” takes the first of several swerves: Instead of charting its protagonist’s first steps into infidelity, it skips breezily through snapshots from the ensuing years-long affair. Andreas becomes almost as entrenched a partner in her life as her husband, though she manages to keep the relationships strictly separate — a rationalized arrangement in her mind, though that collapses when Andreas calmly announces that he’s moving to Greece for a job.

	It’s only with the affair on ice that disorder creeps into Kate’s life, while Orla and their teenage daughter Athena (an excellent Noemi Carbone Mannov) begin to sense something amiss. Editor Julius Krebs Damsbo artfully toggles between present and past, gradually filling in the sensual specifics of the affair — which aren’t entirely as you’d expect — while tracking Kate’s spiraling sense of mourning for whatever it was they had. Without it, her comfortable marriage to Orla seems that much more confined, the increasingly separate islands they seem to be on underlined by DP Maria Von Hausswolff in one tense bedtime argument scene, with the couple’s faces visible only in their respective bathroom-vanity mirrors. Kate seeks solidarity in the aforementioned church group, despite not being much of a believer herself; she doesn’t quite find it, but the candor enabled by all-female company is its own kind of liberation.

	Thorborg Johansen’s subtly nervy performance articulates Kate’s antsy anxieties and erratic moods without making her too much of a scatty romantic heroine. She’s believable while not straining too hard for our sympathy, which winds up fairly evenly divided between all the principals anyway — with a slight advantage to Sears’ beautifully modulated turn as Orla, battling his own emotional and bodily securities while trying to hold down the fort. Handed the most script’s least knowable character, Andersen Lie nonetheless sharply gestures to a life outside his relations with Kate, something she herself hasn’t much considered. In its efforts to be fair to all these characters — via a key, spirit-lightening change of scene — “Brave New Love’s” final act winds up a little fuzzy, though that’s a preferable flaw to tunnel vision: Bäck’s film prefers untidy personal drama to a tidy moral verdict.

schema.headline: ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama

title: ‘Primo Viaggio,’ Presented Last Year at Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development, Has Wrapped and Heading for Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Less than one year after the producers met at the Locarno Film Festival‘s Alliance 4 Development co-development platform, “Primo Viaggio,” produced
body:
Less than one year after the producers met at the Locarno Film Festival‘s Alliance 4 Development co-development platform, “Primo Viaggio,” produced by Italy’s Sacher Film and France’s Halley Production, has wrapped after shooting on location in Naples, Málaga and Marseille between June and July of this year. 

	Written and directed by Alessandro Cassigoli and Casey Kauffman, behind award-winning pics “Californie” and “Vittoria,” “Primo Viaggio” is now bound for the Venice Film Festival’s Gap-Financing Market, where the producers aim to connect with potential sales agents, festival programmers and investors.
	



	

					Mario Di Frenna stars as Carlo in ‘Primo Viaggio.’
									Courtesy of Sacher Film
	



	“Primo Viaggio” (which translates to “First Trip”) follows Carlo, a 20-year-old from Naples who, in an effort to improve his bleak existence, agrees to transport narcotics from Málaga, Spain, back to Italy. It’s the first time he has stepped out of his neighborhood and his insular world, however, and the people he meets while in Spain awaken something within him, leading to a detour that alters the course of his life.


	The project initially came together last year when Andrea Marcelli of Paris-based Halley Production met Sacher Film’s Benedetta Barroero, who is producing alongside Nanni Moretti, at Locarno during the Alliance 4 Development co-development platform for film projects from Austria, France, Germany and Switzerland.

	“We hit it off immediately, and given the film’s story, a co-production with France felt natural and organic,” Marcelli told Variety. “A relationship grew from there that deepened over time into a genuine collaboration, with the directors as well. I’m a French producer but Italian by origin, so exchanges between us are quick and fluid, and also keeping Italian cinema and Italian stories alive matters a great deal to me.”
	

	The project, he added, is “very much in the great tradition of the Franco-Italian co-productions of the past.”

	In making the film, Cassigoli and Kauffman sought to retain the realism that characterized “Californie” and “Vittoria,” which won Venice’s best Italian film prize in 2024. 

	It was those elements that drew Marcelli to the project: “It’s precisely the directors’ method, the way they move between reality and fiction, and their attentive, deeply human gaze on the fate of this young character whose life changes radically through a change of environment. Whether it’s a new place or a chance encounter, this film is about the kind of experience that alters our inner chemistry and allows us to imagine ourselves differently. A universal theme.”

	Cassigoli and Kauffman’s embrace of realism really distinguishes the film, he added, noting that the lead cast, Mario Di Frenna, Sarah-Louna Darnon and Lucky Salvadori, are all non-professional actors.

	“Their cinema starts from reality and feeds off it,” Marcelli pointed out. “Mario Di Frenna, the protagonist, who was cast through a long street-casting process, is a young man who could have lived Carlo’s story exactly, his alter ego in the fiction.”

	The story of Carlo’s first journey abroad also offers an interesting cross-border dimension, he added.

	“The film traces a Mediterranean arc, and we were struck by how much the three cities, Naples, Málaga, Marseille, resemble one another: similar young people, similar problems, but also a shared rhythm and atmosphere.”

	Halley Production’s other recent credits include Manuel Gómez Pereira’s 2025 Goya-winning Spanish hit “The Dinner” (“La cena”), on which it also served as co-producer.

title: Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian yogi and mystic Sadhguru is teaming with Graphic India on “Shiva: The Adiyogi,” an animated feature retelling the origin story of Hindu God S
body:
Indian yogi and mystic Sadhguru is teaming with Graphic India on “Shiva: The Adiyogi,” an animated feature retelling the origin story of Hindu God Shiva as the first yogi. 

	Sadhguru and Sharad Devarajan share story credit on the film.

	Graphic India is the studio behind India’s animated mythology franchise “The Legend of Hanuman.” Devarajan, who co-created that series and co-founded Graphic India, is producing, co-writing and co-creating “Shiva: The Adiyogi.”
	

	The film spans from before creation to the peaks of Kailash, taking in the rage of Veerabhadra, a being formed from grief, and the devotion of two women whose bond keeps Shiva connected to existence. It builds to a scene at Kanti Sarovar in which Shiva imparts 112 methods for transcending physical existence to seven seekers.


	“In the yogic culture, Shiva is not seen as a God. For us, Shiva is the Adiyogi – the first yogi, and the Adiguru – the first guru. For the first time in the history of humanity, Shiva the Adiyogi introduced the idea that the simple laws of nature are not permanent restrictions. If one is willing to strive, one can go beyond all limitations and attain to liberation. Breaking the laws of physical nature is spiritual process. In this sense, we are outlaws, and Shiva is the ultimate outlaw,” said Sadhguru.

	“This is the story of how wisdom itself was born, and why it was shared with humanity,” added Devarajan. “As a storyteller, there is no greater canvas, a cosmic love story, a tale of devastating loss, and action on a scale no epic has ever attempted. Armies of gods fall before a warrior born of pure grief. A blind conqueror storms the gates of heaven. A third eye opens and burns desire itself out of existence. And through all the fury and spectacle runs the most tender story imaginable, of the two women whose love was fierce enough to reach an infinite being, and the final gift he gave humanity because of them. To craft this story alongside Sadhguru, the defining voice of the Adiyogi in our time, is the greatest creative honor I could imagine.”
	

	Sadhguru is also a bestselling author whose videos stream in 35 languages on social media. He founded the Isha Foundation, a nonprofit human-service organization, more than three decades ago; it is now supported by over 19 million volunteers worldwide.

	Devarajan’s credits also include the “Baahubali” animated series, comprising “Baahubali: The Lost Legends” and “Baahubali: Crown of Blood,” and the co-creation of Pavitr Prabhakar, the Indian Spider-Man character for Marvel who appeared in the Oscar-nominated “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.”

	“Shiva: The Adiyogi” is targeting a worldwide theatrical release. Jeevan J. Kang and Subrah S. Iyar serve as executive producers and Navin Miranda and Nayana Bijli as co-producers. Production is being led by Graphic India’s animation studio.

schema.headline: Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India
description:
Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has become the highest-grossing Hollywood film in India, dethroning “Avatar: The Way of Water.”

	A $10.6 million
body:
Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has become the highest-grossing Hollywood film in India, dethroning “Avatar: The Way of Water.”

	A $10.6 million weekend boosted the “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” India total to $52.8 million, according to Sony. “Avatar: The Way of Water” had a lifetime gross of $50.8 million. 

	The result was expected after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” delivered a historic theatrical debut in India, dethroning “Avengers: Endgame” to claim the biggest opening frame for a non-Indian film in the country’s box office history.
	

	The superhero tentpole generated a gross collection of INR72.44 crore ($7.6 million) on its first day, surpassing the previous Hollywood launch benchmark set by “Avengers: Endgame”. The opening frame saw nearly 1 million moviegoers flocking to cinemas on its opening Thursday alone.


	Across India’s largest cinema chain, PVR Inox, the film grossed over INR135 crore GBOC ($14.1 million) during its opening weekend, welcoming nearly 3 million moviegoers at an average occupancy of 60%. Nationwide, the film’s four-day extended opening weekend produced a gross collection of $35.4 million, according to Sony, across 17,250 screens.

	Gautam Dutta, CEO, revenue and operations, PVR Inox Limited, had said about the film’s historic opening weekend: “The response to ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ has been truly outstanding and reflects the enduring appeal of global event cinema on the big screen. What has been particularly encouraging is not just the scale of the opening weekend, but the breadth of audience participation across markets. We have seen exceptional demand from metros as well as Tier II and Tier III cities, with advance bookings, healthy walk-ins and repeat viewership contributing to sustained momentum throughout the weekend.”
	

	Metropolitan centers recorded unprecedented demand, with Bengaluru leading all cities by contributing 23% of tracked top-city grosses, followed by Hyderabad at 17%, Mumbai at 15%, and Delhi at 14%. 

	Linguistic versatility and broad penetration across India’s regional circuits drove the record gross numbers, with strong demand spanning major metropolitan centers as well as Tier II and Tier III cities. The original English-language version led theatrical collections with a 55% occupancy rate across nearly 8,000 shows. The Hindi-language dubbed edition generated an extraordinary 95% occupancy across some 7,000 shows, demonstrating the character’s reach into regional markets. Southern regional language dubs in Telugu and Tamil added further momentum across key circuits.

	The film crossed 6 million ticket sales on ticketing portal BookMyShow on its opening weekend. “The film has struck a chord with audiences nationwide, with English leading the charge, closely followed by Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, while markets such as Hyderabad, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru and Chennai continue to drive exceptional demand. The film is doing superbly in all non-2D formats including 3D, 4DX, Dolby and Epiq formats,” said Ashish Saksena, COO – cinemas, BookMyShow.

	“What’s particularly exciting is that ‘Brand New Day’ has now surpassed the lifetime ticket sales of several landmark titles including ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home,’ ‘Avengers: Infinity War,’ ‘Spider-Man: Far From Home’ and ‘Spider-Man: Homecoming’ on BookMyShow,” Saksena added. “This is a clear reflection of the growing appetite for tentpole cinematic experiences and the unparalleled excitement that beloved franchises continue to generate. The response has been extraordinary, reiterating that when it comes to event films and large-screen spectacle, audiences continue to choose the magic of the theatrical experience.”

schema.headline: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India

title: Germany’s Patra Spanou Film Boards Rodrigo Plá’s ‘The Newcomers’ After World Premiere at Locarno’s Kids Screenings (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Düsseldorf, Germany-based Patra Spanou Film has picked up world sales rights to “The Newcomers” (“Los nuevos”), the latest film from Mexico’s Rodrig
body:
Düsseldorf, Germany-based Patra Spanou Film has picked up world sales rights to “The Newcomers” (“Los nuevos”), the latest film from Mexico’s Rodrigo Plá (“The Other Tom”) in his first venture into kid-targeted films.

	According to Patra Spanou, she acquired it soon after its world premiere at Locarno’s Kids Screenings. “I have been following Rodrigo Plá´s work for a while and I am delighted to start our first collaboration with ’The Newcomers,’” she told Variety.
	

	“With his latest film, he manages to touch difficult subjects like forced displacement, migration and environmental exploitation in an accessible way for children by making a film about friendship and adventure to entertain the whole family.”


	Filmed in Mexico’s striking Tabasco region by DP Ángel Jara Taboada, “The Newcomers” follows three tweens led by Mateo who sometimes breaks the fourth wall as he narrates their adventure. Tiana and her family have sought refuge in Mateo and his brother Tomas’ village but the pollution they have fled has also reached the village. Along with Tiana’s pet dog Nube, they set out to find out what is poisoning the rivers.



	

					The Newcomers
	



	Plá’s sixth feature is an adaptation of the book “They Came with the Wind” (“Llegaron con el viento”) by his regular collaborator, screenwriter and wife Laura Santullo.

	“Indeed, it’s our first film for children and it’s been a challenge. It’s a film that, through adventure, tries to bring complex issues like migration or the importance of protecting water from the greed of mining closer to children. So, the project has meant, on one hand, experimenting with new narrative tools, since it’s aimed at a young audience but at the same time we can recognize in it some of our long-standing concerns, like our interest in social justice or the importance of having a critical spirit about what surrounds us,” Plá told Variety.
	

	He added: “While we’ve brought child characters to the screen before, this is the first time we’ve given voice to a child’s subjectivity. In ‘The Newcomers,’ Mateo is both the protagonist and the narrator. What happens on screen is the memory of a special year when a group of refugees arrived in his town, a year of growth and experiences that he perceives as epic. And that’s how the film tells it, with several narrative nods to the idea that what happens in the images isn’t so much what truly happened, but a subjective reconstruction of events, a tale.”

	The filmmaking couple now have three new projects in development: a musical, a dystopian drama and a black-comedy thriller. “We’ll see which one gets funding first. As you can see, we like to move around, try new things. ‘Los nuevos’ is a clear example of that.”

	Plá, who first broke out with 2007 social thriller “The Zone,” which debuted at the Venice Film Festival, has dabbled in various genres. “But they all have some recurring concerns, like the tension between the public and the private or an interest in social processes, though always told from an intimate place, from the personal experience of the protagonists,” he explained.

	“But really, I think the films one makes change along with oneself; they largely reflect the concerns or interests of each stage of life.”

	“The Newcomers” is a Buenaventura Cine production in co-production with Mr. Miyagi Films. Gabriela Maldonado,  Plá,  Santullo, Ángeles Hernández and David Matamoros serve as producers.

	Patra Spanou Film also had Diego Llorente’s “How the Lights Get In” (aka “Dying Bird”), sneak peeked at this year’s Locarno Spanish Film Previews on Aug. 9, which impressed as the portrait of a younger generation’s recreation of bedrock affective bonds beyond those of a traditional couple. Lara González Lobo at Failo Cine, in Gijón, northern Spain, produces with Báltico (Spain) and Uruguay’s tarkiofilm.

	The 79th Locarno Film Festival kicked off on Aug. 5 and wraps on Aug. 15.

	John Hopewell contributed to this article.



	

					The Newcomers

title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Bests ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’
description:
“The Odyssey” sailed to the top of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Aug. 7–9.

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service
body:
“The Odyssey” sailed to the top of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Aug. 7–9.

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Christopher Nolan-directed epic generated $10.3 million from 1,333,569 admissions over the three-day frame across 1,798 screens, capturing a 45.13% share of total weekend revenue. Since launching wide on Aug. 5, the tentpole has collected $14.4 million from 1,874,863 admissions.
	

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” moved to second place in its second frame, bringing in $9.2 million from 1,264,788 admissions over the weekend. The film captured a 40.38% share of the frame, pushing its overall South Korean cume to $43.7 million from 5,916,425 total admissions.


	Local animated sequel “Teenieping: Legend of the Whale Heartstone” was in third place, generating $1.9 million from 289,464 admissions over the frame. Directed by Kim Soo-hoon, the musical fantasy sequel follows Princess Romi, Heartsping, and their companions as they journey into a deep-sea city to rescue Queen Velita. Counting previews, the film has accumulated $2.8 million from 433,807 viewers. 

	“Hope” finished in fourth place with $748,364 from 100,904 admissions over its fourth weekend. Directed by Na Hong-Jin and starring Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung, Jung Ho-yeon, Michael Fassbender, and Alicia Vikander, the film has now reached a total of $33.2 million from 4,393,885 ticket buyers.

	Faith-based animated production “David” claimed fifth place, adding $111,506 from 16,860 admissions and has a gross of $1.9 million from 289,350 total viewers.
	

	“Minions & Monsters” took sixth place, adding $92,550 from 14,616 admissions for a total of $5.3 million from 763,307 viewers.

	Japanese director Tomoaki Fujino’s family documentary “What Should We Have Done?” placed seventh, bringing in $86,947 from 12,030 tickets over its second weekend frame for a cume of $353,255.

	Toho’s anime mystery entry “Detective Conan: Fallen Angel of the Highway” landed in eighth place ahead of its wide release, pulling in $79,796 from 8,828 admissions across preview screenings. Directed by Takahiro Hasui, the latest film in the franchise follows Conan Edogawa as he investigates a high-speed conspiracy behind a series of deadly highway disasters.

	“Toy Story 5” placed ninth with $43,972 from 6,389 admissions, extending its local gross to $21.3 million from 2,939,376 tickets.

	Rounding out the top 10 was the local action-comedy sequel “OK! Madam: Bon Voyage,” which captured $31,448 from 3,909 admissions across preview screenings. Directed by Lee Cheol-ha and starring Uhm Jung-hwa, Park Sung-woong, Lee Sang-yun, and Sooyoung, the comedy follows a former secret agent whose luxury cruise vacation turns into a high-stakes hostage crisis when a ruthless criminal syndicate strikes. The title has gathered $81,887 from 11,783 total viewers ahead of its Aug. 12 launch.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $22.9 million, making it the biggest weekend of the year, surpassing last week’s $20.8 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Bests ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’

title: Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar Launch Excel Origins, Initiative to Discover Filmmakers Under 30, as India’s Excel Entertainment Marks 25th Anniversary (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Excel Entertainment is marking its 25th anniversary with the launch of “Excel Origins,” an initiative from co-founders Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Ak
body:
Excel Entertainment is marking its 25th anniversary with the launch of “Excel Origins,” an initiative from co-founders Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar dedicated to discovering, developing and backing the next generation of Indian filmmakers under 30.

	Sidhwani and Akhtar were 26 years old when they founded Excel Entertainment and began work on their first film, “Dil Chahta Hai.” The film became a defining title for its generation and set the template for the company’s focus on fresh voices, original ideas and creative risk-taking.
	

	In a joint statement, Sidhwani and Akhtar said, “25 years ago, we started Excel Entertainment and began work on a film called ‘Dil Chahta Hai.’ We had a simple belief – New voices and a different way of telling stories, will find an audience. We were 26 years old. We didn’t have all the answers but we had an idea we believed in, the courage to take risks and the tenacity to make it happen.”


	The founders framed the new initiative as an extension of that founding philosophy, applied to a new generation of talent.

	“As we look back at everything this journey has given us, we also find ourselves thinking about what the next 25 years has in store for us. We believe it will include Excel empowering young, aspiring filmmakers with bold ideas and the courage to tell stories differently,” they said. “So, as Excel celebrates its silver anniversary, we’re launching Excel Origins – an initiative to discover and back the next generation of filmmakers. New voices. Original stories. Breakthrough genres. Because the best way for us to celebrate where we came from is to invest in where cinema goes next. 25 years of Excel. Now, back to our Origins.”
	

	Under the new banner, Excel plans to scout emerging directors and writers, offering them backing and creative latitude to pursue original material rather than proven formats. The company said its search will span multiple genres and storytelling forms, and will extend to casting opportunities for actors and other talent who are similarly early in their careers.

	Sidhwani and Akhtar described the effort as bigger than any single slate of titles. The goal, they said, is to build an ongoing supply line of new directing, writing and acting talent, alongside original intellectual property, that will shape Excel’s output over the coming years, with the company framing the push as a bet on unproven talent at a moment when much of the industry leans on established names and familiar formulas.

	Since “Dil Chahta Hai,” Excel Entertainment has built a filmography spanning “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara,” the “Don” and “Fukrey” franchises, “Raees,” “Dil Dhadakne Do” and “Gully Boy.” The company also produced “Inside Edge,” India’s first original series for Prime Video, and went on to make “Mirzapur,” “Made in Heaven,” “Dahaad” and “Bambai Meri Jaan” for the platform.

title: Aubrey Plaza Welcomes First Child With Christopher Abbott
body:
Aubrey Plaza
                          Welcomes First Baby!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 9, 2026
                
                            4:45 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 9, 2026
                                5:56 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
            Aubrey Plaza is officially a mom ... welcoming her first child with partner Christopher Abbott!
      
    
            Aubrey was seen holding her little bundle of joy on Sunday in New York City after seeing "Death of a Salesman" -- Chris' last performance.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ … Aubrey welcomed a baby girl during the last week of July, making the couple a family of three.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aubrey looking effortless in a high ponytail and chic black sunglasses. Their baby was wrapped snugly in a blanket and beanie … cozied up in the first-time mom’s arms.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... news of Aubrey's pregnancy surfaced in April, with the baby expected to arrive in the fall.
      
    
            The 'White Lotus' star made no effort to hide her growing belly in the months that followed ... stepping out with her bump on display as she prepared to become a first-time mom.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The new arrival marks Aubrey and Christopher's first child together. She was previously married to screenwriter and director Jeff Baena, but they did not have children before their separation and his death.
      
    
            Aubrey and Christopher previously worked together on the 2020 movie "Black Bear" and the off-Broadway play "Danny and the Deep Blue Sea."
      
    
            Congrats to the new parents!!!
